verdicts.name: services/config/config_service.py:1264 process_config_form
verdicts.reason: One-line delegation to ConfigFormParserService.process_config_form, which is not included in source/ for this section - the actual form-parsing logic cannot be verified.

findings.trigger: A file under config/containers/*.json is not valid UTF-8 (or its top-level JSON value is not an object, e.g. a list or a number) -> open()+json.load() raises UnicodeDecodeError or TypeError while reading/parsing it. Neither exception is in the per-file except tuple (json.JSONDecodeError; IOError, OSError, PermissionError, RuntimeError, docker.errors.APIError, docker.errors.DockerException) at line 99/103, nor in the outer except at line 128, so it propagates out of _load_container_configs() uncaught, and therefore out of get_all_servers()/get_valid_containers()/get_ordered_servers()/get_server_by_docker_name() as well - one bad container file breaks the listing of every container, not just the bad one.
findings.suggestion: Add UnicodeDecodeError (and ideally TypeError/AttributeError for a non-dict top-level value) to the per-file except clause, the same way services/config/config_service.py:_load_json_file already does for the equivalent case, so a broken file is skipped and logged like the other 'unreadable' cases instead of taking the whole list down.

findings.trigger: save_container_config()/delete_container_config() are documented to return True/False. Both call _validate_path_safety() (line 26) first, which raises ValueError for a name that fails the safe-name regex or resolves outside containers_dir. Neither method's except tuple (line 100: IOError, OSError, PermissionError, RuntimeError, json.JSONDecodeError; line 126: RuntimeError, OSError, PermissionError) includes ValueError, so an invalid/unsafe container_name makes the function raise instead of returning False as documented.
findings.suggestion: Add ValueError to the except tuples in save_container_config and delete_container_config (or catch it locally around the _validate_path_safety() call and return False), so a rejected name behaves like every other failure mode instead of breaking the documented boolean contract.

findings.trigger: get_config_service() is a 'SERVICE FIRST' method that is supposed to always return a GetConfigResult. Its handling of ConfigCacheError retries once with self.get_config(force_reload=True), but the retry's own try only catches ConfigLoadError (line 1074), not ConfigCacheError. If the cache keeps failing (e.g. a persistent disk/permission problem hit again on the retry's own set_cached_config call), the second ConfigCacheError is not caught anywhere in this method and propagates to the caller as an unhandled exception instead of a GetConfigResult(success=False, ...).
findings.suggestion: Catch ConfigCacheError (and ideally the same broad set used by the outer try) in the retry's except clause too, so a repeated cache failure still returns a graceful GetConfigResult instead of raising out of a method whose whole contract is to never raise.

findings.trigger: control_channel_ids() only reads the legacy 'channels' list (format: list of {'channel_id', 'permissions': [...]}) when the new-format loop over 'channel_permissions' produced zero channels (`if not channels:`). It does not distinguish 'channel_permissions is absent/empty' (a genuine legacy install) from 'channel_permissions is present but every channel currently has control=False' (an operator who deliberately revoked control everywhere). In the second case, a still-present legacy 'channels' entry for a channel that used to have control can be picked up by the fallback and treated as a control channel again for the watchdog's default notice channel and the update notice, even though the current (authoritative) format says no channel has control.
findings.suggestion: Only fall back to the legacy 'channels' list when 'channel_permissions' itself is missing/empty in the config, not merely when it yields no control channels, so a deliberate 'no control channels' state from the modern format is not silently overridden by stale legacy data.
findings.unsure_why: config_loader_service.py and config_migration_service.py (which build the merged config and decide whether/how long a legacy 'channels' list survives) are not in source/ for this section, so it cannot be confirmed whether current installs can actually still carry a populated legacy 'channels' list alongside a populated 'channel_permissions' dict, or how much this affects real deployments versus being a purely theoretical leftover path.

findings.trigger: extract_web_config() builds its whole result dict inside one try block (lines 121-129). 'session_timeout' is int(config.get('session_timeout', 3600)) guarded only by isinstance(value, (int, str)) - a non-numeric string (e.g. session_timeout: "abc") passes the isinstance check but makes int() raise ValueError. Because the conversion happens inside the dict literal, the exception discards every other field that was already computed correctly, and the except clause (line 130) returns get_default_web_config() instead - which sets web_ui_password_hash to None, even though the real value was read from config just fine.
findings.suggestion: Convert session_timeout on its own (try/except just around int(...), falling back to 3600) instead of bundling it with the rest of the dict, so a bad session_timeout value cannot wipe out an unrelated, already-valid web_ui_password_hash (or the other fields) via the shared except clause.
findings.unsure_why: The only caller of extract_web_config visible in this section is the one-time legacy v1.1.x migration path (_migrate_legacy_config_if_needed -> ConfigMigrationService, not in source/), so it is not possible to confirm from this section alone whether a lost password hash here is later restored/merged by the migration service, how often a genuinely corrupted session_timeout occurs in practice, or whether this function is also reachable from somewhere else not shown.

notes: services/discord/__init__.py was included in source/ but has no entries in PLAN.txt, so nothing from it was reviewed or verdicted. Two smaller observations that did not rise to separate findings: (1) ServerConfigService.get_base_directory() calls the full load_config() (all config files, token decrypt) just to read 'base_dir', unlike _load_container_configs() which deliberately avoids that for performance reasons per its own comment - a perf inconsistency, not a correctness bug. (2) status_channel_ids() has no legacy-format fallback at all, unlike control_channel_ids() (F4) - an asymmetry between the two functions in the same file, but not clearly wrong since status_channel_ids only reads the new 'channel_permissions' format. Also, on a first-ever save (no existing bot_token on disk yet), ConfigService._keep_bot_token_encrypted()/_repair_bot_token() both no-op, so whether the very first bot_token ever reaches disk in encrypted form depends entirely on the caller (config_form_parser_service.py / the /setup route, not in source/) calling encrypt_token() before save_config(). SPEC.md states Z9 holds and is tested, so this was not raised as a finding, only flagged as a dependency on code outside this section.
